prompt.context: Emerson is a $10B company that offers landline phone and broadband internet services to an area with 20 million households and businesses. To diversify their revenue, Emerson has decided to enter the television market. They have invested in cable boxes that can be used by homes and businesses to watch TV. Emerson has sought our help to determine their pricing strategy, independent of their existing phone and internet plans, to maximize profit and whether they will be able to successfully beat competitors.
prompt.question: What pricing strategy should Emerson use for their cable TV service, and will they be able to successfully beat competitors?

clarifying_info.q: What is Emerson's current market share in their region?
clarifying_info.a: Emerson has 50% market share in their region.
80% of their customers are households and 20% are businesses.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider pay television network fees (e.g. HBO, Showtime)?
clarifying_info.a: Pay television network rates are set and should not be considered in the pricing strategy.
There are two other companies that provide cable boxes in the area (both smaller than Emerson) and they also compete with DirecTV (satellite TV provider).
The infrastructure is already in place so startup costs are minimal and can be excluded for the purposes of this case.

clarifying_info.q: How does Emerson want to price relative to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Emerson believes they need to be 15% below market prices in order to attract customers.
Emerson wants at least a 25% margin on their services.

exhibits.title: Market Research: Average Prices for Cable Packages of Competitors
exhibits.shows: A pricing grid showing average monthly prices charged by competitors, broken down by number of channels in package (10, 35, 80, 150, 400) versus number of cable boxes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5+), along with the percentage of customers purchasing each channel package.

exhibits.title: List of Variable Costs for Cheetah Cable Television Services
exhibits.shows: A table listing Emerson's variable cost items and their per-unit costs for the cable TV service.

framework: Financial Analysis: Revenue projections, variable costs, margin analysis, NPV/ROI/payback
Market/Competition: Market size, CAGR (growing/mature/declining), market fragmentation, customer preferences and willingness to pay
Company: Current financial health (leverage, revenues), execution capabilities, synergies with existing phone/broadband LOBs, supply chain and supplier relations

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 1: What does the competitor pricing structure tell us about what drives price?
questions.guidance: The price increases more for larger channel packages than for additional cable boxes. The price for the largest TV package (400 channels) is between 3.5x and 5x the price for the smallest package (10 channels). The price for 5 cable boxes is never more than double the price for 1 cable box within the same channel package. Customers tend to purchase 1 or 2 boxes (60% combined). This implies higher costs are associated with package size increases than with cable box increases. Heavy math is not required on this exhibit.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, develop a pricing strategy for Emerson that meets both the 25% margin requirement and the 15% below-market pricing requirement.
questions.guidance: A strong answer builds a base price covering per-account costs, then adds per-box and per-channel rates, each marked up to meet the 25% margin requirement and still land 15% below competitor prices. To meet both a 25% margin and 15% below market, costs must be marked up by approximately 40% (1/(1-0.25) = 1.333; being 15% below market means price = 0.85 * market; so the effective markup over cost is roughly 40% combined buffer). The candidate does not need to price every combination — once the strategy and rates are set, spot-check a few combinations. A key advanced observation: the 400-channel package cannot satisfy both constraints simultaneously.

math.setup: Account base costs = Installation ($5) + Support ($10) = $15. Mark up 40% for margin and competitive pricing: $15 * 1.40 = $21 minimum base price. Per cable box cost = $5. Mark up 40%: $5 * 1.40 = $7 minimum per box. Per channel cost = $0.25. Mark up 40%: $0.25 * 1.40 = $0.35 minimum per channel.
steps: Compare to market for 1 box, 10 channels: $35. Emerson price $31.50 is 10% below market (below the 15% threshold requirement means it qualifies). Check: $35 * 0.85 = $29.75 is the 15%-below ceiling; $31.50 > $29.75, so this just barely fails the 15%-below target — candidate should recognize the pricing needs further adjustment or note the constraint is tight.

Spot check — 1 box, 400-channel package: $21 + $7 + (400 * $0.35) = $21 + $7 + $140 = $168. Market price for 1 box, 400 channels = $140. Emerson price of $168 exceeds market — cannot meet both margin and competitive pricing targets for this package.
math.answer: Emerson can price competitively (within 15% of market with 25% margin) for the 10, 35, 80, and 150-channel packages with 1 cable box, but cannot satisfy both constraints for the 400-channel package.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should Emerson consider when planning to enter the cable TV market?

categories.name: Pricing-related
ideas: Bundling with existing phone and broadband services
Customer segmentation (households vs. businesses have different WTP and usage)
Raising prices over time once market share is gained (penetration pricing strategy)

categories.name: Additional Product Features
ideas: Streaming service partnerships (e.g., Netflix, Hulu integrations)
Revenue and cost synergies with existing phone and internet services
Value of customer data on viewing habits for monetization or targeted advertising

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Poor service quality could negatively impact existing phone/broadband client relationships
New technology could disrupt the market (streaming, 5G, etc.)

recommendation: Emerson should enter the cable TV market in the 1-box category for the 10, 35, 80, and 150-channel packages, as these can meet both the 25% margin target and the 15% below-market pricing competitiveness target.
Emerson should not initially launch the 400-channel package under this pricing strategy, as it cannot satisfy both margin and competitive pricing constraints simultaneously.
risks: Competitors lowering their prices, triggering price wars that erode Emerson's margin
Internet and streaming services substituting cable TV (cord-cutting accelerating)
Implementation and operational risks in standing up a new line of business
next_steps: Pilot the pricing strategy in selected geographies to test sales uptake and operational readiness
Ideate bundling strategies combining the new TV service with existing phone and broadband offerings to increase ARPU and lock in customers
Evaluate whether the 400-channel package can be made viable through renegotiating content costs or adjusting the competitive pricing requirement
